title: The Best Boozy Advent Calendars to Gift This Year
summary:
We have entered the golden era of Advent calendars, and our top picks are filled with wine, beer, spirits, and more.

The post The Best Boozy Advent Calendars to Gift This Year appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
There once was a time when Advent calendars were filled with little cardboard illustrations, or, if you were lucky, cardboard-tasting chocolates. Thankfully, we have entered the golden era of Advent calendars, filled with legitimately exciting gifts: jams, lipsticks, teas, perfumes, macarons, and, best of all, booze. 

For the uninitiated, Advent calendars can be any shape or size, but they always feature 24 to 25 “doors” meant to be opened every day leading up to Christmas, revealing a festive surprise. (There are also 12-day versions that count down to Christmas.) The item has its roots in 19th-century Germany, where Protestants began counting down to Christmas by lighting candles or making marks with chalk on walls or doors. It is believed that the first chocolate-filled Advent calendars emerged in the 1950s, and Cadbury launched its own in 1971.

The lavish themed Advent calendars of today—often exorbitantly priced, like the controversial $825 Chanel Advent calendar of 2021—are a far cry from its humble origins. (We’re not sure how 19th-century German Protestants would respond to the sight of a “24 Days of Rum” Advent calendar, but we suspect they wouldn’t love it.) 

In the lead-up to this holiday season, give the gift of adult beverages. Whatever your loved ones like to drink, whether it’s wine, spirits, beer, or liqueurs, there’s a calendar for it. These are the 13 best boozy Advent calendars we could find this year.

Note: These items sell out quickly every year, so don’t procrastinate too long.

In Good Taste: 2026 Wine Advent Calendar

This annual best-seller is packed with 24 bottles of whites, reds, and rosés from around the world. Each bottle is 6.32 ounces, or 187 ml—i.e., a generous glass. The Advent calendar also includes daily tasting videos to guide your tasting experience.

$137 In Good Taste

In Good Taste: 2026 Red Wine Advent Calendar

For an arguably more seasonally appropriate selection of wines, this red wines-only option makes another wonderful gift. The reds are sourced from France, Italy, Napa, Sonoma, Paso Robles, and beyond.

$150 In Good Taste

Vinebox: 12/24 Nights of Wine

Choose an Advent calendar with 12 or 24 nights of wines, and then choose between styles: The Velvet Collection features “eight sumptuous reds and four elegant whites,” while the Vine Collection contains a lively mix of “expressive reds, distinctive whites, and a radiant rosé.” Note that these come in 100 ml containers, which is less than the standard 187 ml.

$139 or $229 Vinebox

Hallmark Channel Wines: Advent Calendar

That’s right, the Hallmark Channel makes wines, and of course they come in Advent calendar form, with 24 mini bottles of red, white, sparkling, and rosé. Each bottle contains 187 ml of wine, which equates to a solid glass.

$130 Hallmark Channel Wines

Just Enough Wines Holiday Advent Calendar

The Just Enough Advent calendar is a great choice for the California wine lovers. It features 12 premium wines from the Golden State’s Central Coast including reds, whites, and bubbles. The generously-sized 250 ml cans provide a large single-serving or a small pour for two. To add to the festive feelings, the calendar also comes with a guide to food pairings and seasonal activities.

$125 Just Enough Wines

Costco: Wine Calendar

The annual Costco Wine Calendar tends to sell out quickly, and you can’t purchase it online, but we would be remiss if we didn’t include one of the most coveted wine Advent calendars. Like most things Costco, the value is exceptional: the calendar contains 24 375 ml bottles, rather than the standard 187 ml. According to Costco Wine Blog, this year’s offering features France most prominently with six bottles, but a wide range of other countries are represented, including Spain, the U.S., Chile, Italy, and newcomer North Macedonia.

$100 Purchase in store, while supplies last

WSJ Wine: Advent Calendar

This 24-bottle Advent calendar sells out every year and includes reds, whites, rosé, and Prosecco in 187 ml portions. Some highlights of this year’s offerings are Il Papavero Prosecco; Sonnenstrahl 2025, an exciting Grüner Veltliner from Austria; and Belle Roche’s acclaimed Cabernet Sauvignon.

$160 WSJ Wine

Total Wine: Wine Adventure Advent Calendar

It should come as no surprise that one of the biggest wine retailers on earth has entered the wine Advent calendar game, with 24 bottles, sized 187 ml. From zooming in on the product image, we spot a Spanish red blend, German Riesling, French rosé, and plenty of other globe-trotting goodies.

$90 Total Wine

Flaviar: Whiskey Advent Calendar

Taste whiskeys sourced from all over the world in the month leading up to Christmas. You’ll find plenty of the usual suspects, like award-winning American rye, single malt Scotch whisky, and Kentucky bourbon, but we’ve also spotted French and Indian selections, too. The calendar comes with two collectible Glencairn glasses and an interactive tasting pamphlet. 

$270 Flaviar

Give Them Beer: Beer Advent Calendar 2026

We can’t think of a better gift for beer lovers than this 12-can craft beer Advent calendar, which features IPAs, stouts, ales, and more of the site’s top-selling beers. The gift also clocks in under $100, unlike some of the more elaborate versions.

$89 Give Them Beer

The Spirit Co: Gin Advent Calendar

This cute U.K.-made gin Advent calendar ships to the U.S. and is filled with 25 top gins from around the world, plus two tasting glasses and a journal with expert tasting notes.

$135 The Spirit Co.

The Vermont Country Store: Abtey Prestige Liqueurs Adult Advent Calendar

No need to choose between a traditional chocolate Advent calendar and a boozy one: this jolly option is stocked with liqueur-filled dark chocolates featuring Rhum St. James, Gin Gibson, Poire Williams, Kirsch Cherry, Cognac Bayet, Whiskey Label 5, and Irish Coffee. The little chocolates come in festive barrel, fruit, and bottle shapes.

$50 The Vermont Country Store

Del Mesa Liquor: 24 Days of Rum World Tour

For the spirits lover, this calendar featuring 24 rums from 24 countries is an excellent choice. It comes with two tasting note booklets and two glasses, so it makes a particularly nice gift for couples.

$120 Del Mesa Liquor

title: Central Coast Innovator Gretchen Roddick Is Wine Enthusiast’s Person of the Year
summary:
The executive vice president of Hope Family Wines has helped shape the Central Coast wine scene for decades.

The post Central Coast Innovator Gretchen Roddick Is Wine Enthusiast’s Person of the Year appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
As the daughter of two blue-collar entrepreneurs, Gretchen Roddick learned early on what it takes to succeed in any industry.   

“You work hard, fail fast, then get up and do it again,” said Roddick, who is being honored with the Wine Star Award for Person of the Year. “I really take pride in the work ethic I was taught growing up.”

No surprise that the executive vice president of Hope Family Wines and board chair of the Wine Institute started working at age 14. “There’s never been a day that I haven’t had a job,” said Roddick.

Initially starting as a tasting-room host for Hope Family back in 1997, she’s helped the company grow from just 1,000 cases of wine to nearly one million today, which are distributed in all 50 states and 62 countries. Among numerous other volunteer positions, she joined the Wine Institute—which promotes California wine at the national and international levels—as a regional director in 2008, became an officer in 2023, and serves as the board chair through 2027.

“I’m doing the same thing I did from day one: I’m leading by example,” said Roddick. “I represent the wine business. I speak from the heart. I speak authentically about agriculture, jobs, and tourism.”

Roddick may have never gotten into wine if her parents hadn’t encouraged her, as a teenager, to leave a lucrative sales gig at Nordstrom’s in San Jose and go to Cal Poly in 1990. After graduating with degrees in fruit science and agricultural business, she studied Spanish in Cuernavaca, Mexico, then returned to the Central Coast, working in the cellar of regional bubbly pioneer Maison Deutz (now Laetitia). “I dragged hoses,” she said. “I crushed grapes.”

She moved to Paso Robles in 1995, and was hired by Treana winery two years later. When her college classmate Austin Hope walked through the door a month later, she learned his family owned the business. His parents, Chuck and Marlyn Hope, took an immediate liking to Roddick, and asked her to learn the wine business alongside their son. 

“They saw something in me,” said Roddick fondly. “They embraced a journey I had no idea I could be doing. I’m so proud to have been working alongside Austin Hope. We just got up every day and we did it.”

What they did varied widely. Hope Family sold off its first tasting room quickly in order to grow into a national brand, and then returned to focus on the direct-to-consumer experience a decade later. Today, they are all of the above, an international player with two stylish tasting rooms in Paso Robles. Every step of the way, they’ve turned to Roddick to execute Austin’s creative vision. 

“If you don’t know how to do it, Gretchen is not afraid to do it,” Roddick said of how it’s gone for 30 years. “She will figure out a way.”

She wears many hats—promoting Hope Family, Paso Robles, the Central Coast, and California at large—but employs a similar strategy for all. “It’s important to go out and listen,” she said. “We have two ears and one mouth.”

One of her favorite roles is speaking to Cal Poly’s incoming class of wine students. “I speak about their journey and what they can do,” she said. “There’s a place for you. You just gotta find it.”

Roddick clearly found hers, and she’s nowhere near done. “I told Austin, ‘We have 20 more years,’” she said. “There’s a lot to do. We can make a difference. We’re only halfway there.”

title: The Race to Snap Up Grosses Gewächs Rieslings Has Begun. These Are the Bottles to Watch
summary:
Grosses Gewächs (GG), Germany’s equivalent to France's grand cru vineyards, produce bottles that are coveted by collectors around the globe.

The post The Race to Snap Up Grosses Gewächs Rieslings Has Begun. These Are the Bottles to Watch appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
At this year’s Grosses Gewächs (GG) preview in Wiesbaden, Germany, the strongest wines carried little evidence of the anxiety behind their production. The 2025 Rieslings were often generous yet energetic, the 2024 reds increasingly individual, and the later releases among the most complete wines on the table.

Germany’s GGs, the dry wines from the country’s highest-ranked vineyards, offer an annual snapshot of the country’s ambitions. This year, they also revealed the nimbleness and flexibility of top German producers. Earlier harvests demanded faster decisions, while increased overall ripeness allowed growers to reconsider typical approaches to balance.

The established names delivered. Alongside them, estates such as Schlumberger-Bernhart, Knewitz, and Rings, as well as those led by younger generations who have taken over family wineries, made a persuasive case for widening the conversation.

The 2025 Rieslings: An Early Reckoning

Of the regions represented, the Mosel and Rheingau were less consistent than I had hoped this year, though their strongest wines remained among the tasting’s highlights.

Florian Lauer, proprietor and winemaker of Weingut Peter Lauer in the Saar, began harvesting on September 7, his earliest yet. He remembers harvests starting in mid-October during his childhood. The shift brings particular difficulties to steep vineyards, where picking cannot simply accelerate to outpace the changing climate.

Compact Riesling bunches are vulnerable to rapidly spreading rot, he explains, while warmer harvest conditions create challenges for a region accustomed to bringing in cooler grapes.

For Matthias Knebel in Winningen, September rain transformed an otherwise steady growing season into a race.

“We started September 15 and finished the harvest in just 16 days,” he says.

At Winningen’s Uhlen vineyard, picking began on September 17 at 102 degrees Oechsle, a German measure of sugar ripeness. 102 degrees is equivalent to an auslese wine, without the influence of botrytis.

“A great blessing of this vintage is the pronounced and energetic acidity, which beautifully supports the ripeness,” says Knebel.

His experience reinforces a growing imperative: once grapes are physiologically ripe, waiting for higher sugar readings risks losing the balance already there.

Lauer is also reconsidering his production methods. His GGs contained less than two grams of residual sugar per liter and underwent full malolactic fermentation. He favors warmer fermentation and savory complexity over overt fruitiness.

“We try to bring out the spiciness,” he says.

His Riesling Kupp showed that approach beautifully, combining clementine and white raspberry flavors with silkiness and flinty detail. Saarfeilser was more savory, with floral complexity and a long, salty finish.

Meanwhile, Clemens Busch’s Marienburg married stone fruit with crunchy freshness, Kühling-Gillot’s Ölberg was expansive and vibrant, and Wittmann’s Aulerde stood out for yellow fruit and a brilliant saline finish. Generosity rarely meant heaviness among the strongest wines.

The Reds: Differences That Matter

The 2024 reds offered considerable quality despite the season’s difficulties. Fürst’s Hundsrück had firm structure and a long future ahead. Meyer-Näkel’s Pfarrwingert brought cherry flavors and silkiness. Franz Keller’s Achkarrer Schlossberg layered black tea, hibiscus, and pomegranate notes, while Rings’ Felsenberg was polished and floral.

As a category, German Pinot Noir can be inconsistent. However, among these producers, quality is largely the starting point.

Beurer’s later-release 2023 Mönchberg Öde Halde illustrated that beautifully, its cherry, raspberry, and red currant unfolding through flowers and spice. The wine’s appeal lay in its ease and detail, with neither acidity nor tannin interrupting its flow.

Cellarmaster Adrien Beurer made adjustments in the winemaking process, including the use of whole bunches, but maintained continuity in the vineyard. “In farming, we didn’t change anything,” he says.

Württemberg also supplied outstanding Lembergers. Schnaitmann’s 2024 Lämmler combined blackberry and sandalwood notes with fresh acidity and substantial but melting tannins, an example of the region’s impressive ambitions.

The 2024 Whites: Worth the Wait

Peter Jakob Kühn releases its GGs a year later than most estates. Its 2024s made an excellent argument for that patience.

“Cool nights brought precision and focus, while balanced rainfall and healthy soils gave natural depth,” says Peter Bernhard Kühn, the winery’s current head.

Kühn’s Mittelheimer St. Nikolaus was rounded and composed, with yellow fruit, flowers, and a stony finish. “It has depth without weight, complexity without excess, and an effortless sense of flow,” Kühn says.

His Hallgartener Jungfer was a highlight for me: flinty, saline, and rounded, with prominent acidity held in remarkable balance.

In Baden, Schlumberger-Bernhart’s cellarmaster Johanna Bernhart also found much to admire.

“2024 was a very wet and cold year, but it provided excellent conditions for cool, mineral-driven white wines,” she says.

Schlumberger-Bernhart’s Altenberg Weingarten Weißburgunder, Grauburgunder, and Chardonnay shared freshness and salinity while retaining distinct personalities. The Chardonnay was particularly compelling, with white raspberry and orchard blossom notes, and taut structure.

Odinstal’s unconventional Riesling and Schnaitmann’s electric Götzenberg were also notable. Together, these wines suggested that a GG report is increasingly a story of individual decisions: when to pick, how to ferment, and when to release. The vineyard supplies the possibilities. The grower must recognize which ones the year will allow.

Standout Wines

Peter Lauer Riesling Kupp GG 2025 (Saar)

Lightly flinty, with clementine and white raspberry unfolding across a silky palate. Fine texture and sustained flavor distinguish this beautifully balanced Riesling.

Clemens Busch Riesling Marienburg GG 2025 (Mosel)

Orchard blossom and stone fruit meet a flinty edge. Bright acidity and a crunchy texture bring freshness without diminishing the generous fruit.

Knebel Riesling Uhlen GG 2025 (Mosel)

Generous ripeness meets pronounced, energetic acidity in this refined Riesling. Its concentration is balanced by freshness and elegance.

Kühling-Gillot Riesling Ölberg GG 2025 (Rheinhessen)

A lightly reductive opening reveals white raspberry, papaya, flowers, and exotic spice. Generous in flavor, with flinty detail and mineral vibrancy keeping the palate focused.

Wittmann Riesling Aulerde GG 2025 (Rheinhessen)

Flinty notes frame white raspberry and generous yellow fruit. Expressive and finely balanced, this finishes with pronounced salinity and impressive persistence.

Peter Jakob Kühn Riesling Jungfer GG 2024 (Rheingau)

Flinty reduction introduces a deeply saline Riesling with a rounded, medium-bodied palate. Prominent acidity is beautifully integrated, bringing precision to a wine of considerable texture and depth.

Odinstal Riesling GG 2024 (Pfalz)

Green melon and tangerine candy give this distinctive Riesling an unconventional appeal. Incisive acidity and a crunchy mineral texture keep it lively through the long finish.

Schlumberger-Bernhart Chardonnay Altenberg Weingarten GG 2024 (Baden)

White raspberry and orchard blossom meet flinty notes in this saline, finely balanced Chardonnay. Tension and freshness give the palate particular distinction.

Rudolf Fürst Spätburgunder Hundsrück GG 2024 (Franken)

Pure fruit and floral notes unfold across a rounded palate. Firm tannins and underlying tension give this a substantial framework for aging.

Franz Keller Spätburgunder Schlossberg GG 2024 (Baden)

Black tea, hibiscus, dark cherry, and pomegranate give this Pinot considerable complexity. Supple tannins support the fruit through a long, layered finish.

Rings Spätburgunder Felsenberg GG 2024 (Pfalz)

Elegant and polished, with floral notes and dark berries finely woven together. Baking spice adds detail through a long, composed finish.

Beurer Spätburgunder Mönchberg Öde Halde GG 2023 (Württemberg)

Cherry, raspberry, and red currant mingle with flowers and spice. Elegant and lively, with beautifully integrated acidity and tannins and a long, multilayered finish.

Rainer Schnaitmann Lemberger Lämmler GG 2024 (Württemberg)

Blackberry and black currant meet sandalwood spice in this fresh, expressive red. Substantial but silky tannins provide structure without weighing down the palate.

The Room

Create the envelope

Insulation, vapor protection, doors, glass and adjoining spaces all affect how difficult the cellar is to keep stable.

A cellar with extensive glass, for example, may require substantially more cooling than an insulated room of the same dimensions. Wine Enthusiast’s cooling guidance therefore treats room construction and heat load—not cubic footage alone—as part of selecting a system.

The Climate

Create the environment

Wine cellar cooling equipment is different from ordinary room air conditioning. It is designed to maintain the steady temperatures needed for wine while accounting for the moisture conditions of the cellar.

The right cooling technology depends on the room, where heat can be exhausted, how visible you want the equipment to be and the demands of the project.

Build around the collection

Good racking does more than hold bottles. It determines how efficiently the room stores wine, how easily you can find a bottle, what you choose to display and how the cellar can grow.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should I choose a custom wine cellar instead of a wine fridge?

A custom cellar starts to make sense when your needs extend beyond the capacity or footprint of a large refrigerator—particularly when you’re considering several large units, want room for significant collection growth, or want wine storage to become part of the architecture of your home. Bottle count matters, but the available space, how you organize the collection and how you want to use the room matter just as much.

Does every wine cellar need a cooling system?

Not necessarily. A naturally cool, stable cellar may already provide appropriate storage conditions. Most purpose-built wine rooms inside modern homes, however, require dedicated climate control because ordinary residential HVAC is not designed to maintain wine-storage conditions consistently.

How do I know which cooling system my cellar needs?

Cooling-system sizing depends on more than room volume. Insulation, glass, adjoining temperatures, ambient conditions and where the system can exhaust heat all affect the cooling load. For that reason, Wine Enthusiast recommends a consultation before purchasing a cellar cooling unit.

No. EuroCave offers premium racking and the INOA cellar-conditioning system, and those products can be incorporated where they suit the project. title: People Still Want Wine at Their Gatherings—but Gathering Is the Challenge
summary:
According to a new survey, people still want wine on the table. It’s just a matter of finding the time (and budget) to gather.

The post People Still Want Wine at Their Gatherings—but Gathering Is the Challenge appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
The wine industry is plagued with discourse about deflating sales. But a new study, backed by Come Over October (in partnership with Local Wine Events), sheds light on some of the untapped opportunities that could help the wine industry not only survive, but thrive. 

“We were looking into what’s behind the downturn,” says Gino Colangelo, co-founder of Come Together and president of Colangelo & Partners. “How can wine address it?”

As the survey of over 1,500, both non-drinkers and wine drinkers showed, people are still interested in wine—even if their spending behaviors don’t always reflect that. The majority of respondents (61%) say that wine is almost always part of their social get-togethers, and 41% of respondents cited “occasions” as their main impetus for drinking wine: birthdays, promotions, milestones, break-ups, girl’s nights, even Vanderpump Rules premieres.

“It all circles back to the idea that people need an occasion,” says Colangelo. 

Getting together, however, isn’t always so easy. 77% of respondents cited busy schedules as the main reason they weren’t gathering, and 40% cited the distance between friends and loved ones. It can feel too expensive, time-consuming, and physically taxing to gather.

“Sometimes in their busy lives, they don’t find enough reasons to get together and drink wine,” he continues. Colangelo, alongside veteran writer Karen MacNeil and marketing powerhouse Kimberly Charles, founded Come Over October as a campaign to encourage those social occasions people are craving, but struggling to organize. “It’s an easy banner in which people can gather.”

The Good News: People Still Like Wine

Despite what all the headlines suggest, people still want wine on the table.

The survey dug into how people feel about wine in social situations. Respondents were shown two tablescapes: one with wine on the table and another with water in its place. When respondents were asked what moods came to mind when they saw the table with wine, the most frequent response was “fun.” Others shared “good time,” “friendship,” “connection,” and “togetherness.” By and large, surveyants found that wine made the scene look warm and relaxed.

The bottom line is that people consider wine an occasion- and food-based beverage, so it needs to be marketed accordingly. Wine should meet people where they are: in shoebox city apartments watching Heated Rivalry with friends, or sitting around their coffee table and splitting styrofoam boxes of takeout. 

Drinkers were intrigued with wine and expressed openness to adopting more drinking occasions, but they needed to be told how. 32% of respondents said they were looking for wine recommendations, specifically for varying budgets and occasions.

The Big Barriers to Gathering

Many of the findings may be obvious to industry members—of course people drink wine at parties. Other data points underscored that, even years after a global pandemic, people are struggling to rebuild their social lives. In fact, 26.49% of respondents said they were going out less than they did a year ago. 24% of respondents are too stressed out by the thought of hosting to have friends come over. 

This data is consistent with social trends that have been in motion for decades, long before the pandemic. ​A DDB Needham Life Style survey shows that between 1975 and 1998, the share of Americans who hosted or attended a monthly dinner party declined by half. In the following 30 years, the United States has seen double-digit declines in almost every measure of socializing—attending sporting events, volunteering, and going to bars. 

Piling onto the post-pandemic shake-out are new barriers, like the current cost of living crisis. It’s expensive just to exist right now, let alone socialize. We live in an age where $25 glasses are becoming the norm. Understandably, 33% of respondents credited financials—cost of living, cost of drinks—as a major prohibitor to buying wine. 

The impact of the economic climate is shifting the volumes people buy wine in and the velocity people dine out at. Instead of going out for dinner, KPMG’s 2026 Consumer Pulse survey found that 67% of U.S. consumers are eating at home more often, with 76% of those consumers citing budget constraints as a primary reason.

“Economics are a factor—you’ve noticed a dearth of time, dearth of cash,” says Colangelo. “But getting together doesn’t have to entail an expensive restaurant.”

title: How NBA Legend CJ McCollum Turned Wine into the Family Business
summary:
McCollum and his wife, Elise, join the WE Podcast to discuss running a family vineyard, the bottle(s) they'd pop if the Hawks took home a championship, and why the NBA is embracing wine.

The post How NBA Legend CJ McCollum Turned Wine into the Family Business appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
This past spring, the world watched as one man brought the New York Knicks to the edge of playoff elimination. Atlanta Hawks guard CJ McCollum rattled off 26, 32, and 23 points in games one, two, and three of their first-round series, respectively. The Knicks were on their heels. 

New York fought their way back—all the way to an NBA championship (check out what bottle Josh Hart opened to celebrate). Regardless of how the series played out, it’s safe to say that McCollum made quite the impression on Knick fans, including myself.

Entering his 14th year in the league, McCollum is an NBA legend. In 2013, he was drafted 10th overall by the Portland Trail Blazers, after cementing his legacy at Lehigh University as the Patriot League’s all-time leading scorer. He’d go on to take home the NBA’s “Most Improved Player” award in 2016, and would serve as president of the National Basketball Players Association from 2021-2025.

He’s also, as you might’ve guessed, a wine guy.

Over the years spent living and playing in Portland, McCollum and his wife, Elise, developed and solidified a love for Oregon wine. In 2017, the McCollums partnered up with Adelsheim Vineyard to create their own wine, releasing their first bottling in 2020—Heritage 91. Seeing the success of this project, the couple purchased a 318-acre property in Oregon’s Yamhill-Carlton AVA in 2021, paving the way for the launch of their own winery, McCollum Family Vineyard.

The couple joined me on the Wine Enthusiast Podcast to chat about their wine journey, what it’s like balancing family life and an NBA schedule, and what bottle (or bottles) they’d pop if CJ took home an NBA championship this year. Listen to learn more.

On What Made CJ a Wine Lover

CJ McCollum: “Yeah, I mean, I didn’t like wine. I was more of a spirits guy in college, heavy on the spirits, and being in Oregon, being in the valley, it was an eye-opening experience just to kind of see what was out there. But I always joke—I didn’t like wine, but I liked Elise. And in my pursuit of her, and then just also organically being in Oregon for so long, it allowed us to just gain exposure naturally and organically. And then curiosity continued to pique and it really started with her introducing me to wine through her parents.

And then being able to taste, you know—Walter Scott Pinot from Bryan Creek Vineyard was the first Oregon Pinot that I ever tasted, at Ringside Steakhouse from James. And from there it was just more about, you know, learning, growing, asking questions. I started doing a ticket exchange with sommeliers, with servers at different wineries and just began to kind of build out a network that we felt would be helpful for us in our development of the wine space, but also just organically would happen based on conversations that we have at different wineries. And Elise and I would enjoy date nights, we enjoyed date days, trips where we just go out and just dive into the cellars and dive into the barrels and do barrel tastings and just ask questions. And the science behind it, I think, was fascinating to her. I think it was fascinating to me as well. But then the hospitality side of the storytelling, the relationships that you build, how present you are… I think all of those things kind of played a factor in our growth in this space.

But it’s also—when you’re not drinking quality wine, and I don’t mean like expensive wine, I mean just like well-made wine, it’s hard to appreciate it when you’re younger. But as you continue to learn and you start to see the sustainability efforts and you see the growth that has taken place in Oregon and the types of varieties you can drink and then how there’s, you know, hundreds and hundreds of wineries who are doing things the right way, making a great product, it kind of opens your eyes to the the environment that you didn’t necessarily grow up around.”

On how Adelsheim Vineyard and a Fellow NBA Star Showed CJ the Beauty of White Wine

Elise McCollum: “[Heritage 91] first started in 2017, we started purchasing grapes from Adelsheim and evolved to our first release in 2020, which was just our Pinot. And it was a lot of fun. You know, you work on the branding, you work on the partnership with Adelsheim—we learned so much in those years from them, and it just really sparked our interest and kind of grew from there. I remember, initially, CJ was thinking about, ‘Should we do another wine? Should we not?’ He’s like, ‘Well, I don’t drink Chardonnay, so we’re not gonna do that, so let’s continue with Pinot.’ And I remember then… CJ, if you want to tell the story with Carmelo that kind of piqued your interest with Chardonnay.”

CM: “Yeah, so I was historically a Pinot guy and I would do bubbles. We had a rosé which was 100% Pinot Noir, so it still kinda fell underneath that Pinot tree. And they kept asking if we wanted to buy fruit to make Chardonnay. And I was like, ‘I don’t like still Chardonnay, so I don’t really feel comfortable making it and selling it to people and trying to get people to buy something that I’m not, you know, really sold on myself.’

And we had bought fruit to make a Blanc de Blancs, which was cool because it was bubbles and, you know, we were in that realm of just enjoying bubbles, you know, freely, not just celebratory, but just in general. And then ‘Melo, a friend of mine who, you know, ended up playing with us in Portland, I introduced ‘Melo to Oregon Pinot and he introduced me to White Burgundy. And when we sat down and drank some White Burgundy together, I was like, ‘Okay. I do like Chardonnay and I can make a Chardonnay, but it has to be eerily similar to this Burgundian approach and style.’ 

… It’s safe to say that we both enjoy Chardonnay now. Not just in the summertime. Throughout the year we’ll drink Chardonnay pretty often.”

On the Financial Realities of Owning a Winery

CM: “I think we struggle to come to terms with lots of things, especially when it’s labor, it’s financially intensive, but it’s also time: You can make more money, but you can’t create more time. And I think that’s something that you learn as you continue to grow and continue to develop in any space—a yes to something is a no to something else. So, how much time can we truly put into this to make it successful? It’s already a tough industry. It’s an expensive industry. It’s labor intensive. It’s financially intensive, especially building something from scratch.

… Yeah, whenever you’re doing something new and something that you’re not an expert in, there is gonna be some pause for sure. But the principles are the same, you know? Customer service, hospitality… making sure everybody enjoys their time with us, I think, is really, really important. The level of service, the product, and the types of experiences that we can create, I think are authentic. Obviously, it’s a good time, but I think they’re repeatable things that we can do consistently and those are things that we can actually control.

We can’t control the market. We can’t control a lot of things that are being written about the industry, but we are having some success. And there’s a lot of wineries that are having some success. They’re able to sell wine, able to provide great experiences for people, and they’re making great products. And I think where the industry is at now is that it’s weeding out the people who aren’t serious about it or don’t have a really great product. You need a good product, you need to be serious about it. And the storytelling is vital in order to have success, especially now in this type of market. But we’re building organically, we’re building slowly, and we’re still a long way away from where we want to be, but I think we’re taking the right steps and we’re heading in the right direction. And it starts with doing things the right way, having a great product, and providing people with great experiences.”

On Making McCollum Family Vineyard a Family Business

Jake Abrams: “On the McCollum Family Vineyard website, you have Jacobi [their son] listed as a Rock and Soil Foreman and Margaux [their daughter] as the Chief Grape Sampler. Do you see them as being involved in the future?”

EM: “Absolutely, 100%. And that was one of the main reasons why CJ and I decided to pursue this as much as we did—we saw this as something for our entire family to be involved with. So for CJ and I to be able to work together… we always felt like with our individual careers and our family life, we individually didn’t get to spend time together. So this is something that really brought the two of us together to be able to work on, and then also, as the kids are growing, become involved with the vineyard side of things.

So, coming out to the vineyard every year, they absolutely love it. It’s something that they can be involved in for their entire lives if they want to. As of now, they love it. They can’t wait to go to Oregon. My son was telling everybody that would listen to him that he couldn’t wait to go. And it’s so cute to see. And you know, it’s their childhood, so you want them to be so excited to do different things. And for us it’s just wonderful to be able to include the entire family. If we couldn’t, I don’t think that we would have been able to do it because, you know, you want to spend as much time as possible with your family. So it really worked out.”

On the Wine(s) CJ Would Open if the Hawks Win the NBA Championship

CM: “Man, I don’t even… That is a great question. I’d probably go New World first. I’d probably open a New World Oregon Pinot. I might—I’d go back as close to my birth year and as close to Elise’s birth year as we could get. Let’s start with that, and then we probably go Old World. Our daughter’s name is Margaux, so that’s an easy one. Find something there, and then Elise likes Super Tuscans, so we may go there. But I mean, I’d have to check the cellar. Just… put it like this: I can assure you it’ll be more than one bottle consumed and it wouldn’t just be wine if we won a championship.”

On Why the NBA and Its Players Are Gravitating Towards Wine

CM: “I think it’s… culturally in the NBA, it’s a lot more acceptable. When I first got into the league, it was frowned upon to drink or to have, you know… sponsorships with potential alcohol beverages weren’t as prevalent. But I think now you see there’s Modelo, there’s all those big brands that have individual sponsorships with players and it’s become more approachable. But I think dating back to, you know, what I said in the beginning, the sports world is heavy on camaraderie, breaking bread, and having dinners, you know? Having nights out with your teammates, with your staff, coaches’ dinners, players’ dinners, all-staff dinners. I’ve been on teams where there’s a dinner invitation in every city. I usually pick the restaurant in a lot of cities based on how long I’ve been in the league and the types of relationships that I have.

But the league is big on communion and breaking bread. So, like, in that respect it makes sense why wine has continued to become more prevalent and more popular. It’s also more socially acceptable because the president of the team is probably, you know, enjoying himself a glass of wine or herself a glass of wine. The ownership groups may enjoy themselves wine as well. And it’s something that we all can kind of relate to, obviously, you know, being over 21. The league has gotten younger, so a lot of younger guys aren’t able to participate. But they can still go and have a nice dinner and get a mocktail or get some tea. I’m a big tea guy. So there’s still a lot of ways for that to happen. But I think the culture of sports is big on communion. It’s big on hospitality. It’s big on people going out and enjoying themselves because we play at night a lot of times. So at night, what do you do after the game? You can’t wind down. You have to go eat. You have to replenish, refuel. And then you land in the next city and you’re landing in time for dinner and you want to watch sports or you want to watch a TV show. You unwind with eating and occasionally you’ll have a beverage alongside that.”

The Guests

CJ and Elise McCollum are the co-founders and co-owners of McCollum Family Vineyard, an estate-driven Oregon wine venture established in 2026. Rooted in stewardship, sustainability, and a long-term commitment to the Willamette Valley, the vineyard reflects the McCollums’ estate-driven vision for crafting wines shaped by intentional farming, family legacy, and a genuine expression of place. Blending their distinct professional backgrounds—CJ’s as an NBA player and Elise’s as a pediatric dentist—the couple has built their approach to wine around curiosity, family, and a shared desire to create something enduring for future generations.

It’s safe to say that we both enjoy Chardonnay now. not just in the summertime. Throughout the year we’ll drink Chardonnay pretty often.

JA

Yeah, awesome. Yeah, I feel like a lot of people have a gut reaction when it comes to Chardonnay and there’s just so much out there. But with Adelsheim, how did that partnership start? You know, how did you decide that these are the people and this is the land that we want to buy grapes from and this is the winemaker that we want to work with?

CM

Yeah, so Adelsheim actually reached out to my agency about a potential collaboration and began to just kind of talk about what it would look like. And it started with us creating a label. They knew that we enjoyed Pinot. They knew that I was a huge Pinot fan historically, but didn’t really drink anything else. And they were like, ‘why don’t we just start with Pinot?’ So we kind of sat down and we mapped out a plan where there would be just a good education and learning around it. And we basically said that we would like, you know, bi-weekly immersive learning where we’re able to learn about the soil profile, able to learn about clones, able to learn about the barrels, medium versus light toast, how you age the wines, how the weather kind of impacts that, and how the winemaker has control over manipulation of the wine, but the wine obviously is gonna speak for itself. So there was immersive learning for Elise and I alongside Gina on the actual winemaking side. We began to taste different clones to kind of understand what the clones are like by themselves, what they’re like together, and how you blend certain types of clones together, and then introducing stainless steel, how you play with, you know, how much new French oak you’re introducing to the wine. So there was immersive learning there where we slowly grew, asked a lot of questions and we had continuous conversations about how it’s very imperative that she talks to us as if we’re in the third grade from a developmental standpoint. I was like, ‘you don’t leave anything out. That’s really important for us. Like we’re starting from scratch. So we need to know all the nuances of making this product.’

And then from there we began to meet with Rob, who’s the president of Adelsheim, but that was more about the business of wine. Like, how do we hire strategically? How do we enter markets? What does the licensing look like? If we want distribution in new states, what does that look like for us? and it was just really helpful to be able to see, you know, a winery that’s been around, the first winery in Chehalem, you know, fifty, sixty years of existence of doing things the right way at this point in time. They were completely honest with us, they were up front, they were very instrumental, helpful in our development in this industry and in this business. We inherited all their licenses to be able to sell alcohol from the very beginning. So it was really, really helpful. And you know, I credit them, and I think Elise would say the same thing, in our introduction to wine in Oregon specifically and how to run a business effectively, how to hire effectively from a strategy standpoint. And then I’ll never forget the conversations we had before we, you know, began looking at properties and purchasing our own property. And Rob basically told us everything. And then in the end he was like, you know, ‘You sure you wanna do this? Like I don’t necessarily think this isn’t something you should do, but if you’re gonna do it, this is how you do it,’ type of thing. And we laughed all about it and I said, ‘This is something that we’re really passionate about’ and we understand, you know, the wine industry has a saying, you know, if you wanna make a million, you gotta spend ten. And sometimes they’re pretty accurate with that. But I think all in all, it’s a passion. There’s a real love here and this is something that we’re proud of and this is something that we’re gonna make a legacy, you know, for our kids and things beyond us that will last. But it’s about how you treat the earth, how you treat your fruit, how you treat your team members. And I think we’re doing things the right way and organically building exactly what we said we would build while staying true to who we are and our foundational pillars.

JA

It’s so cool to hear you say that. It feels safe to say that this was not something that you just saw as a marketing opportunity or slapped your name on. Like, it seems like you’ve really been in the weeds, you know, no pun intended, involved very heavily since way early on.

CM

Yeah, and I mean I’d let Elise speak to, you know, the development and the processes that we’ve gone through from, you know, hiring staff to continue to figure out ways to learn more, continued education, all those things. I’d let her speak to it and then I would just briefly just talk about how encompassing the wine industry is. There’s so many parts to it. It’s fascinating.

EM

Yeah, yeah. Just like CJ said, there’s so many facets to it. It’s extremely interesting. I feel like I always say this was never something that we, you know, we went to a vineyard one day and we said, ‘Let’s start a vineyard.’ Like this… it really grew. This passion really grew from the start and each year progressed more and more into a stage where we really wanted to lay down roots and start something for ourselves and for, like CJ said, for generations to come. So it’s a passion that really has grown year after year to get us to this point.

CM

Yeah, and just to follow up and to give you a little bit of background, ’cause I know you’ve probably heard about the things that we’ve done, but I mean, it started off as a Christmas tree cattle farm. So it’s not like we purchased an existing vineyard. We had to learn strategically about, you know, what types of clones we want to plant, what types of rootstocks. We had to kinda go through the process of understanding the environment, understanding our soil profile. We had to figure out, you know, did we have the right types of water rights? You know, now we’re building a taste room. So you’re going through a wetland survey, you’re going through the architectural steps that are necessary to understand the square footage and what the square footage means for your parking lot. How many bathrooms do you have to have on property? So you have like the whole gambit of things that involve the actual wine. There’s the actual business of wine, the licensing that’s required to sell alcohol in different states. Every state has different licensing rules. It’s like marriage dates. There’s all these things that you have to go through and hoops that you have to jump through to physically sell wine. You have to learn about the shipping aspects of wine. You have to learn about the actual labeling, the bottling, design, the cost, you know, the cost on foil versus no foil. What types of corks do you use? You know, what color bottle do you have for your Pinot versus your Chard versus your rose? What type of celebratory labeling would you like on your sparkling wine, the back copy? Sll those things are hugely a part of the industry and a part of the business, and it doesn’t go unnoticed.

Understanding the entire business is really important for development and also important for how you figure out what types of team members are necessary for your success. But I mean, without a team, this isn’t possible. And Elise and I, we know our strengths and our weaknesses and we try to support each other the best ways that we can. But we’re very involved in the operational side of the business in terms of strategy, structure, how we do events, where we do events, the timing of events, the dinners, the tastings, from the flowers that are picked out strategically to the types of tablecloths to the types of chairs, the customization of our airstream that we have on property right now, the tastings that we started three weeks ago. Elise and Natalie spearheaded that. That’s not my department. That’s not something I’m very good at. It’s just about understanding like where you can kind of get in where you fit in at. And I like to be out in market. I like to drag the bag. I like to meet with sales teams. I like to do staff training when we get a new account on the road. Those are things that I’m good at. But it’s also understanding, you know, what do you need to get better at? What do you need to learn about– Elise has a license to pour, so she pours the events. I don’t have my license to pour. I need to get it. So those are things that you just have to kind of grow and learn.

But I mean, we’re a part of the business. We’ve dived into it and have continued to learn it. We don’t have all the answers. And the good news is that the valley has been very helpful and instrumental in our development. So many wineries have helped us on, from Granville, to Stoller, to Soter to Sequitur. There’s so many people. Ken Wright has reached out. There’s so many people who have been helpful in our development and allowed us to ask questions, allowed us to kind of get a better understanding of their sales strategies, how they go to market, how they launch. They’re a lot of people exporting wine out of the country now. We obviously distribute our wine in nine states. We were D2C up until 2025 and we just launched nine states over the last fourteen months. So that’s a lot of market work that’s necessary. That’s a lot of learning new environments, what types of wine California likes versus Texas and New York. But it’s been really fun to learn, to grow, to continue to build out our team and to face many challenges in the industry. There’s a lot of challenges, but I think when you have a great story and a great foundation and you build organically and you have a great product, I think all those things matter.

And the last thing I’ll touch on is sustainability and how we treat our fruit and our farm and our team members. I think all of that is very important. We’re Salmon-Safe. We’re LIVE certified. I serve on a LIVE certified board and we really care about equitable wages and we really care about our environment and making sure that it’s, you know, left better than it was when we found it.

JA

That’s awesome. Yeah. There are a lot of challenges in the wine world right now. It’s amazing to hear about how many people have reached out to you guys and been so helpful to you. It’s that kind of time where we need that kind of thing.

Sort of to that point, CJ, I was watching an interview that you gave with Forbes, which sort of went a little bit viral on NBA Reddit about the realities, the financial realities of, you know, of the NBA and budgeting and and how you have managed to take care of money over your career. And you seem like a person who is methodical and is really thinking through that kind of thing. Was the decision to purchase a vineyard, was that something that you struggled to come to terms with, or was that… was it automatic?

CM

I think we struggle to come to terms with lots of things, especially when it’s labor. It’s financially intensive, but it’s also time. You can make more money, but you can’t create more time. And I think that’s something that you learn as you continue to grow and continue to develop in any space is: a yes to something is a no to something else. So how much time can we truly put into this to make it successful? It’s already a tough industry. It’s an expensive industry. It’s labor intensive. It’s financially intensive, especially building something from scratch. But we built in some real support systems and guardrails to kind of prevent certain things from occurring, from you know, using Wells Fargo farm & agriculture as a fiduciary, to strategically building out a three-year, five-year, seven-year, ten-year plan from how much we planted to when we planted, how we staggered our planting, starting with seven acres of Pommard and kind of slowly introducing new fruits that we felt like we could have success making wine, but also selling wine. So playing farmer as well, we do sell some fruit to Adelsheim and to Stoller and some other vineyards. So that gave us some optionality, some flexibility, but in this type of industry, I think there are always worries because of the consumption and how the market can kind of play. But when you have a good product, you have good storytelling and you diversify, I think those are things that allow you to have success. You know, we don’t rely solely on D2C. We don’t rely solely on wholesale. You know, we mix it up based on the markets and based on our approach. And now that we have a designated tasting space, that’s really working out in our favor so far. 

But we’ve started slowly. We started with just buying pinot, then when we were buying some rose, we bought some Blanc de Blancs, slowly introduced new SKUs, slowly expanded into new markets. And now we’re expanding and really honing in on our distribution. And Georgia’s the last state that we expanded in from a wholesale standpoint.

So yeah, whenever you’re doing something new and something that you’re not an expert in, there is gonna be some pause for sure. But the principles are the same, you know, customer service, hospitality, making sure everybody enjoys their time with us, I think is really, really important. The level of service, the product, and the types of experiences that we can create, I think are authentic. I think they’re obviously a good time, but I think they’re repeatable things that we can do consistently and those are things that we can actually control. We can’t control the market. We can’t control a lot of things that are being written about the industry, but we are having some success. And there’s a lot of wineries that are having some success. They’re able to sell wine, able to provide great experiences for people and they’re making great products. And I think where the industry is at now is that it’s weeding out the people who aren’t serious about it or don’t have a really great product. You need a good product, you need to be serious about it. And the storytelling is vital in order to have success, especially now in this type of market. But we’re building organically, we’re building slowly and we’re still a long way away from where we want to be, but I think we’re taking the right steps and we’re heading in the right direction. And it starts with doing things the right way, having a great product, and providing people with great experiences.

JA

Awesome. Yeah. speaking of, you know, the storytelling and your story, I mean… this can’t be unstressful. I mean, you’re gonna be in Atlanta this year, probably going back and forth to Oregon and, like, with your jobs, I mean—Elise you’re a dentist, a pediatric dentist?

EM

I’m a general dentist, but had worked at children’s hospital while we were in New Orleans.

JA 

Amazing. Okay. Yeah. So how do you, you know, as a couple raising a family, how do you navigate this whole thing?

EM

I think within our family, just with each other, delegation with areas, you know, that relate to family life, pretty much full time with our kiddos while CJ’s in season. And with the wine side, we have dedicated time that we set aside for meetings, emails. I mean, the wine stuff is a passion. It’s a huge passion for us. So, making sure we have dedicated time that this is all done the right way and the way that we want it is super important to us. So that’s always very high priority on our list. And then, you know, of course, family time is number one. So fitting those two things in, and then with everything outside, we have a fantastic team in Oregon. Natalie and Ryan are the most wonderful teammates you could ever ask for. And so having teammates like that is irreplaceable and so vital to the wine side that it’s that huge support for our business out there in Oregon. And like I said, we’re in constant communication. So it’s easy to do when you love it, it just becomes… it’s easy. And CJ and I help each other out all the time. We’re teammates. So I think all around having a fantastic team is the most important thing. And then for dentistry, I just got my license in Atlanta, so in the state of Georgia. So hopefully soon I can—

JA

Congratulations!

EM

—start. Thanks! I can start looking for a job soon here. So we’ll figure, you know, you figure everything out. When you want to do something, you figure it out.

JA 

Yeah. It seems like you guys have figured it out. You wanted to do it and you figured it out. Yeah.

EM

We try, every day we try.

JA

Speaking of, you know, on your website, on the McCollum Family Vineyard website, you have Jacobi listed as a rock & soil foreman and Margaux as the chief grape sampler.

EM

Yes.

JA

How do you see them evolving to, you know, be part—do you see them as being involved in the future?

EM

Absolutely, 100%. And that was one of the main reasons why CJ and I decided to pursue this as much as we did. We saw this as something for our entire family to be involved with. So for CJ and I to be able to work together, we always felt like with our individual careers and our family life, we individually didn’t get to spend time together. So this is something that really, like, brought the two of us together to be able to work on. And then also, as the kids are growing, becoming involved with the vineyard side of things. So coming out to the vineyard every year, they absolutely love it. It’s something that they can be involved in for their entire lives if they want to. As of now, they love it. They can’t wait to go to Oregon. My son was telling everybody that would listen to him that he couldn’t wait to go. And it’s so cute to see. And you know, it’s their childhood. So you want them to be so excited to do different things. And for us it’s just wonderful to be able to include the entire family. And we… I don’t think that, if we couldn’t, I don’t think that we would have been able to do it because, you know, you want to spend as much time as possible with your family. So it really worked out.

JA

Of course. Yeah. Switching gears a little bit, I just have a couple more questions. So CJ, you’ve talked previously about how you’d want to make wine less intimidating and more accessible to people. I feel like that’s such an important thing these days, and I just wondered if you could speak a little more to that.

CM

Yeah, I think it stems from upbringing. How we all were raised is different innately, where we come from, our experiences, our parents’ experiences a lot of times rub off on us and I didn’t come from a household where wine was consumed. In the neighborhood it wasn’t consumed as well. So being able to see vineyards for the first time, taste in a tasting room, be out where the cell service doesn’t work as well. There could be animals running around. It was a really cool feeling and a unique experience that I wanted people from, you know, different walks of life to be able to have. And it wasn’t just about the experience. It was also about how when I would go out to eat, after tasting at a vineyard, the comfort level that I would have with the menu started to shift. It wasn’t because I knew everything there, it wasn’t about wine, it was just because I had tasted wine in different places and I felt more comfortable, you know, looking through the menu, getting more comfortable with, you know, New World versus Old World, white versus red. Just the very basics.

But I began to get more comfortable and then I thought to myself, you know, having a vineyard, having a tasting or having a designated space for people to come and enjoy wine, it’s not just about pricing. It’s not about having low prices or high prices, it’s about the experiential aspect of it. Where I’m from, you know, even in church they used to say, ‘Come as you are’ and I think we provide the type of environment where you can come as you are. You can come in sweatpants, you can come in a polo, you can be in, you know, suspenders, overalls, or you can be in loafers and still feel comfortable just being whoever you are. And I think that’s the type of environment that we want to create. And I think when people come taste at our space underneath the oak trees, I think they get that. You know, we’ve had people come in hoop shorts, people bring babies, 10 year olds, nine year olds. We have a suggestion box for the kids so that they can write out things that they would like to see on our property so we can make sure it’s immersive and fun for the entire family.

But so there’s different ways you can approach the industry. And I think for us it’s about family. It’s about experiences. It’s about hospitality. It’s about providing a high level of service. We care about our members, we care about our club members, we care about our first time guests. You know, we track the numbers on everything. We want to make sure that the experience is what it should be. So we stagger our seatings, we don’t rush people out. We make sure that you have a really good time and it’s enjoyable. And you can go tell your friends and your family and your peers about that experience. But for me, it started with that. And I think for Elise it’s the same thing. It’s understanding that this space can be intimidating. It’s suits, it’s white gloves, there’s sommeliers, it’s all these things that you struggle to pronounce at times, but it’s really just about enjoying quality wine with people that you care about. And I think when you take out the rest of it, you really just enjoy the conversations that you have when you’re consuming wine. You enjoy the food and you enjoy those environments. And we have our dinners and our tastings and our interactions on property and off property, we try to reiterate the same things. Like we’re passionate about this and we’re very, very big on hospitality and providing people with great experiences that they can remember forever. And those are impactful moments that we want to carry on. And I think the people that have come to our property and just experienced our brand in general would reiterate those same things.

JA

Yeah, that’s awesome. We’ve seen the NBA recently develop a pretty serious wine culture. Why do you think so many players have gravitated towards wine?

CM

I think it’s… culturally in the NBA, it’s a lot more acceptable. When I first got into the league, it was frowned upon to drink or to have, you know, sponsorships—potential alcohol beverages weren’t as prevalent. But I think now you see there’s Modelo, there’s all those big brands that have individual sponsorships with players and it’s become more approachable. But I think dating back to, you know, what I said in the beginning, the sports world is heavy on camaraderie, breaking bread, and having dinners, you know, having nights out with your teammates, with your staff, coaches’ dinners, players dinners, all staff dinners. I’ve been on teams where there’s a dinner invitation in every city. I usually pick the restaurant in a lot of cities based on how long I’ve been in the league and the types of relationships that I have. But the league is big on communion and breaking bread. So, like, in that respect it makes sense why wine has continued to become more prevalent and more popular. It’s also more socially acceptable because the president of the team is probably, you know, enjoying himself a glass of wine or herself a glass of wine. The ownership groups may enjoy themselves wine as well. And it’s something that we all can kind of relate to, obviously, you know, being over 21, the league has gotten younger, so a lot of younger guys aren’t able to participate. But they can still go and have a nice dinner and get a mocktail or get some tea. I’m a big tea guy. So there’s still a lot of ways for that to happen.

But I think the culture of sports is big on communion. It’s big on hospitality. It’s big on people going out and enjoying themselves because we play at night a lot of times. So at night, what do you do after the game? You can’t wind down. You have to go still eat. You have to replenish, refuel. And then you land in the next city and you’re landing in time for dinner and you want to watch sports or you want to watch a TV show. You unwind with eating and occasionally you’ll have a beverage alongside that.

JA

Yeah. Yeah, that makes sense. A few months back we asked Josh Hart what his most prized bottle was and what he would open if the Knicks were to win the championship. If the Hawks were to go all the way this year, what are you cracking open? I’ll give you a sec.

CM

Man, I don’t even… we got two cellars. We have the home cellar and then we have one in Oregon. That is a great question. I’d probably go New World first. I’d probably open a New World Oregon Pinot. I might—I’d go back as far as close to my birth year and as close to Elise’s birth year as we could get. Let’s start with that and then we probably go Old World. Our daughter’s name is Margaux, so that’s an easy one. Find something there and then Elise likes Super Tuscans, so we may go there. But I mean, I’d have to check the cellar. Just… put it like this: I can assure you it’ll be more than one bottle consumed and it wouldn’t just be one if we won a championship.

EM

Yeah.

JA

For sure. Yeah. Do you guys have similar tastes in what you like to drink?

EM

So it’s interesting to bring that up. We actually differ a lot when we do our tastings, for example. So our winemaker, if it’s during the season, will send us nine different samples for, say, Pinot. And CJ and I will blindly taste everything and write down, you know, all of our thoughts on each of the samples, and then we compare at the end. And we almost always kind of conflict with what we like about each one.

And so it’s really interesting to work with Gina, our winemaker, because she always finds this balance between what the two of us like. And it always ends up being something that the two of us both enjoy so much. So she’s really, really talented in winemaking and at really achieving both of our style preferences.

JA

That’s awesome. Last question. You have built this family business. Where do you see it going in the next 10 to 20 years? What legacy would you like it to leave?

CM

Twenty years is a long way away, so maybe we start with five.

EM

Yeah.

CM

I mean five years from now, I would be forty. I think it’ll be, you know, standing on the foundational pillars that we’ve always talked about, which is, you know, family oriented, you know, taking care of our land, taking care of our team members, experiential, where there’s really cool experiences that are family oriented on property. We’ll have a tasting room that’s open and operating a brick and mortar at that point. We’ll have a brick and mortar by 2029.

But we’ll have the experiential aspect, we’ll have expanded distribution, and we’ll probably be distributing our wines in, I don’t know, fifteen to twenty states that we’ve hand selected that makes sense for us. We’ll probably be exporting wine out of the country at that point. We’ll probably be doing that by 2030. But I think it’s just more about organically building out our property in the ways that we said we would, where we offer many different types of experiences, not just experiences on the hospitality and wine side, but a kid friendly part of our farm. We have a 318 acre farm, a kid friendly part of it where kids are able to, you know, have fun, feed animals, do those types of things, have ice cream, have kid friendly, approachable meals, I think it is really important. We’ll have a hospitality component on property where we’re able to do multi-course dinners, you know, for our members and our guests. I think that’s extremely important to us. There’s a wellness side that’s probably closer to our ten year mark. Big on yoga, Elise is big on fitness and health and just making sure we’re taking care of ourselves. Obviously, we do enjoy the wine industry, but we also want to live long enough to enjoy it. So it’s about health and wellness as well. Where there’s hikes, there’s immersive things like yoga, Pilates. I’m gonna build out a little wellness space, if you will, where there’s saunas outside, outdoor saunas and cold plunges.

This is a little bit down the way, but it’s coming. Time is flying. So I think from that aspect, those are things that we’ve always talked about. And being able to have a one-stop shop. We do own and operate a nursery on property, Ruby Nursery. We sell Japanese maples, hybrids, ginkgos, being able to have a flower shop, Elise can speak to the flowers in the farm and the farm to table aspects. But I think it’s an immersive place that people can come to from all walks of life, all ages, and have a good time, whether you participate in drinking alcohol or not.

EM

Yeah, CJ kind of touched on really diversifying the land and just kind of picking different areas of interest to both of us and things that are important to both of us. So one of the major areas that we plan to do is create a massive garden. So we’ll have an area for herbs, for veggies, for fruits, and then also for fresh cut flowers. So we’re hoping to have like a ‘cut your own flower’ area, as well as like this immersive garden where you can just walk through with your wine, you can enter a greenhouse, or you can just enjoy it at a picnic table and really just enjoy being outdoors. So definitely having this huge garden that as CJ said, you can do farm to table as well, just to incorporate it in all aspects of the vineyard and just as a part of your experience are really important to us.

CM

Yeah. And I think the last thing is, you know, McCollum Family Vineyard is about our family, it’s about our legacy. So producing estate wines and having an optionality to be all-estate if we want to be. There’s some great fruit in the valley, there’s some great older fruit that pairs really well with our young wines, so for now we are still buying some fruit. But I think at some point an all-estate model is not out of the realm of possibility because we do have 56 planted acres and wine is developing fast and it’s tasting well early. So I think we’re pretty confident in the fact that we’ll be able to have our wine stand alone on their own sooner than later.

JA

Awesome. Well, I’m so excited for the future. Thank you guys so much for being here. This was amazing. Thank you so much for making the time. I really appreciate it.

EuroCave HARMONIE

When Wine Belongs
In the Room

A refrigerated wine credenza designed for the spaces where you gather. EuroCave Harmonie combines two temperature-controlled wine compartments with the proportions and finishes of contemporary furniture, keeping reds, whites, rosés and sparkling wines ready to pour.

Explore Harmonie
Talk to a EuroCave Specialist

Designed for the room where wine is enjoyed

A wine refrigerator doesn’t have to live in the kitchen or disappear into a cellar. Instead of finding a place to hide your wine refrigerator, Harmonie makes wine part of the room.

Harmonie brings wine into the living space with a low, horizontal profile inspired by the proportions of a credenza. Behind its doors are two refrigerated wine compartments. Between them, an open central niche creates space for glassware, a decanter, books or the objects that make the room your own.

Ready when you are

Your aging cellar protects the bottles you’re saving. Harmonie keeps the bottles you’re ready to enjoy close at hand and at the right temperature.

43–54°F | Whites, rosés & sparkling wines. The left compartment can be independently set for wines best enjoyed chilled.

54–65°F | Red wines. The right compartment keeps reds within their ideal range for serving.

Up to 50 bottles | One beautifully organized collection. Universal shelving accommodates a variety of bottle formats, so Champagne, Burgundy, Bordeaux and other bottle shapes can share the same space.

Shop readymade configurations

Please allow 16-20 weeks for delivery, direct from France.

title: This African City Is Becoming the World’s Next Drink Capital—on Its Own Terms
summary:
Accra has become West Africa’s most exciting cocktail hotspot, thanks to a rising bar scene that emphasizes Ghana’s indigenous spirits.

The post This African City Is Becoming the World’s Next Drink Capital—on Its Own Terms appeared first on Wine Enthusiast.
content:
Ghana’s cocktail movement and culinary prowess are not anything new to folks with an eye on Africa’s rising popularity in the beverage industry. But Accra, the country’s bustling capital, is continuing to level up. The city has become one of the world’s most exciting cocktail hotspots, thanks to a rising bar scene that emphasizes the city’s culture at its heart. 

Expect to find hyperlocal ingredients like baobab, aidan fruit, and sobolo hibiscus juice, as well as Ghanaian spirits brands like Reign Rum, on cocktail menus across the Greater Accra area, including at Kozo, an Afro-Asian restaurant in Dzorwulu. At Bella Dolce Vita, a popular bar tucked inside a condominium complex, guests sip on a deliciously thick and herbal palm wine gin and other housemade palm wine spirits.

Then, there are the distillers. Surrounded by fruit-bearing calamansi trees and monstera leaves larger than my torso is One Corner Distillery, part of One Corner Garden, a restaurant, guest house, and entertainment venue. Run by Nana-Kofi Appiah and Ezra Davis, the distillery is addressing Ghana’s food waste issues by creating spirits out of produce that would usually be sent to a landfill. Their collection includes palm spirits, rums, and multiple fruit brandies like pineapple, banana, and mango.

A growing number of festivals and exhibitions are only fueling the momentum. The Accra Bar Show, co-founded by Stephen “Kojo” Aidoo in 2024, features locally owned spirit brands, cocktail competitions, and numerous talks and panels on the breakthroughs (and setbacks) of Africa’s spirits industries. The event has drawn bartenders from award-winning addresses in Kenya, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Nigeria, Italy, and other countries for guest shifts in Accra.

At the heart of Accra’s international cocktail moment is a long, rich history of spirits and drinks culture—one that was complicated by colonialism but restored by locals.

The Deep Roots of Ghanaian Spirits

While the buzz is new, Ghana’s drinks culture certainly is not. 

British colonial rule began in Ghana in 1874 (then called the Gold Coast) and lasted until independence in 1957. During that time, many African cultural activities were banned or demonized, including the production of indigenous spirits. The most documented among them is Akpeteshie, a distilled palm wine spirit that goes by many names throughout West Africa—even within Ghana, depending on the language. 

In the 1930s, the British banned Akpeteshie to protect the income the colonial government reaped by importing European spirits and liquors. As a result, the spirit eventually came to symbolize the anti-colonial resistance. Its name, in the Ga language of Ghana, means “they are hiding,” referring to the act of concealing the drink.

After liberation, bars across Ghana began to serve Akpeteshie more openly. Some of today’s bars like The Republic Bar & Grill, which opened in 2012, have made it their mission to celebrate the complex history of this spirit through craft cocktails. Their most popular drink is the Kokroko, a refreshing cocktail with sobolo, mint, lime, and an Akpeteshie base. They also serve an array of infused variations like coconut and vanilla, passionfruit, and coffee-cacao. 

While it’s the most well known, Akpeteshie is not the only pre-colonial spirit in Ghana. “Akpeteshie holds a prominent place in Ghanaian spirit history,” said Aidoo, who is also the founder and president of Bartenders Guild Ghana. “However, Ghana’s pre-colonial beverage landscape is rich in both fermented and non-alcoholic drinks: nsa fufuo, pito, asaana, sobolo, and atadwe milk.”

Nsa fufuo, literally meaning palm wine in the Akan language of Ghana, is the sweet, freshly tapped juice from palm trees that ferments sharply. Pito is a slightly sour and earthy low-abv fermented beer crafted from sorghum or millet, predominantly brewed in Northern Ghana. Asaana is a caramelized, lightly fermented corn beverage made from sprouted corn, traditionally served cold with milk. 

Ghana’s non-alcoholic beverages are just as alluring. Sobolo, a drink made from dried hibiscus leaves and spiced with Hwentia (grains of Selim) and ginger, is beloved throughout the global Black diaspora, including in the Americas and the Caribbean. Atadwe milk (also known as tiger nut pudding) is a non-alcoholic extract made from soaked and blended tiger nuts that offers a naturally sweet, creamy profile.

Flexible and adaptable, palm spirits can be transformed into an assortment of drinks with their own distinct flavor and texture profile, much like how agave, sugarcane, grains, and rice serve as the bases for spirits that are included in the wider alcohol canon. Paving the way for innovation are bars like Bella Dolce Vita, creating gins and vodkas with palm spirits, and One Corner Distillery, experimenting with fruit-infused versions of this age-old spirit.

The Biggest Barriers to Global Recognition

While recognition of Ghanaian cocktail culture—and, specifically, the one in Accra—is growing, there are still systemic barriers to the broader adoption of local spirits and ingredients.

According to Aidoo, there are four hurdles to international recognition of Ghanaian palm spirits: supply chain and quality standardization, import tariffs and inflation, formal education and certifications, and intra-African trade struggles. 

While some of these issues require political intervention, such as the regulatory impositions and high shipping tariffs even between neighboring countries, Aidoo and his compatriots are doing what they can to help Ghanaian spirits professionals pave a way to a brighter future.

The Bartenders Guild Ghana works to create accessible and standardized beverage education for the next generation of bartenders. International beverage shows create opportunities for new distillers and up-and-coming bartenders within continental Africa to gain experience, share their talents, and build necessary bridges within the larger beverage community, while also alleviating some of the financial burdens placed on African professionals by visa fees and travel costs.

The missing piece seems to be wider buy-in from the spirits industry, and that kind of investment has to come from within. As Alexander Quest, the co-founder of Abidjan Cocktail Week in Côte d’Ivoire, puts it, “We must decolonize what success looks like.” 

When Quest first started out, he says the bar scenes in Africa did not elevate local spirits like Akpeteshie the way that the scene does now. He asserts that the industry shift begins by seeing African spirits not as novelties but as drinks on equal footing as the likes of mezcal and vodka. The same goes for the people that make the drinks, shaping Africa’s ever-developing cocktail scene. 

“I want our bartenders to be valued the way they uplift a chef from Paris,” Quest says. “Because what they represent, the work they do, it’s incredibly precious.”

In a world where little is known about the vastness of African spirits and beverages, local bartenders are both service professionals and historians. They create interactive spaces to taste and engage with beverages that have longstanding historical—and sometimes spiritual—significance.
